# Tidal Energy: Harnessing the Rhythm of the Ocean

Tidal energy converts the predictable rise and fall of ocean tides into
electricity. Unlike wind or solar output, tidal cycles can be forecast
years in advance from well-understood orbital mechanics, which makes tidal
generation one of the more schedulable forms of renewable power.

## How It Works

Two broad approaches dominate current tidal technology:

1. **Tidal stream generators** resemble underwater wind turbines. Anchored
   to the seabed, their blades turn as tidal currents flow past, driving a
   generator housed in a sealed nacelle.
2. **Tidal barrages** dam an estuary or bay, letting water pass through
   turbines as the tide fills and empties the basin. Barrages can generate
   substantial power but also reshape local sediment flow and estuarine
   habitat, so recent development has favored smaller, less disruptive
   stream and lagoon designs.

## Site Selection

Good tidal sites share a few traits: a large tidal range (the vertical
difference between high and low tide), a narrow channel or strait that
concentrates current speed, and reasonably shallow water for practical
turbine installation and maintenance access. Coastlines with funnel-shaped
inlets tend to produce the strongest currents, since the same volume of
water is forced through a narrowing passage.

## Engineering Challenges

Saltwater is corrosive and biologically active, so tidal hardware must
resist both corrosion and biofouling — the buildup of barnacles, algae, and
other marine organisms on submerged surfaces. Maintenance crews typically
need specialized vessels and diving or remote-operated equipment, since
components sit on the seabed rather than on an accessible tower. Grid
connection can also be costly where good tidal sites are far from existing
transmission infrastructure.

## Outlook

Because tidal patterns are so predictable, planners can integrate tidal
output into a grid's generation mix with more confidence than with
intermittent sources. Costs remain higher than mature renewables such as
onshore wind, but pilot arrays in several countries continue to refine
turbine design, moorings, and maintenance logistics.
